questions.prompt: Ten minutes into a demo, the owner says, “I just want to see the schedule, then I’ll think about it.” Which part of an up-front contract would have prevented the “I’ll think about it”?

options.text: Agreeing on how long the call would run before you started
Asking what they wanted to see before you shared your screen
Agreeing up front that a clear yes or no at the end is fine
Confirming which competitor they’re comparing you against

questions.reveal: Most AEs set time and agenda. Agreeing on the ending is what stops “I’ll think about it.”

questions.prompt: An owner joins and says, “I only have 20 minutes, not 45.” What’s the best move?

options.text: Re-set the contract: ask what matters most and agree the next step
Speed through the full demo so they still see every feature
Ask to reschedule for a time when they have the full 45
Skip discovery entirely and go straight to showing pricing

questions.reveal: A shorter call needs a new agreement: what to cover and what happens at the end.

questions.prompt: What does good rapport look like at the start of a demo?

options.text: Several minutes of small talk before any business comes up
A joke about their current software to warm them up
A compliment on their website before you share your screen
A brief, genuine question tied to their business, then move on

questions.reveal: Short, real and about their business. Rapport that runs long eats the time you need for pain.

questions.prompt: You open with, “At the end, if it’s not a fit, just tell me. That’s totally fine.” Why does this help the AE?

options.text: It makes the prospect feel obligated to buy by the end of the call
It lowers pressure, so they’re honest about concerns along the way
It lets you skip discovery since they’ll tell you what they need
It shortens the demo because they’ll end the call when they’re done

questions.reveal: Permission to say no makes people tell you the truth earlier, which is where deals are won.

questions.prompt: An owner says, “Our current system works fine. It’s just a bit slow at the front desk.” What’s the best next question?

options.text: “Which system are you on, and how long have you used it?”
“What does slow look like on a busy Monday night?”
“Would you like to see how fast our check-in is?”
“How many front desk staff are on each shift today?”

questions.reveal: “Fine” hides the pain. Ask what slow looks like in real life, then you’ll know what it costs.

questions.prompt: Which question goes deepest on pain?

options.text: “What’s your biggest challenge with your current software?”
“Is there anything you’d change about your current setup?”
“What features are you hoping to see in today’s demo?”
“What has that cost you in clients or hours this year?”

questions.reveal: The first three find the problem. Only the last one finds what it costs them.

questions.prompt: Early in the first call, an owner mentions private events are “a huge part of my business,” then moves on. What’s the best move?

options.text: Stop and dig: how events run today and what that costs them
Note it down and plan to cover events on the follow-up call
Show the events page quickly, then return to your usual order
Wait to see if they mention it again before you spend time on it

questions.reveal: In one of our demos this exact line was never explored, and it turned out to be the deciding need.

questions.prompt: Why dig for pain before demoing, not after?

options.text: It makes the call run longer, which builds a stronger relationship
It lets you skip the screens that every prospect always wants
It lets you tie each screen to something they told you mattered
It gives you time to check which add-ons they can afford first

questions.reveal: Pain first means every screen answers something they said, so the demo lands.

questions.prompt: You ask what they spend on software today, and the owner says, “I’d rather not say.” What’s the best response?

options.text: “No problem. I’ll just walk you through our pricing then.”
“Totally fine. What would make the switch not worth it?”
“Most studios your size pay about $300, so let’s use that.”
“Roughly, is it under $200 a month or closer to $500?”

questions.reveal: A range is easy to answer and still gives you the anchor you need before pricing.

questions.prompt: An owner pays $225 a month for their software. You quote $475 without asking anything else. What did you miss?

options.text: Offering an extra free month before you shared the price
Their full spend: add-ons, third-party tools, fees and time
The date their current contract renews or ends this year
Which add-ons their nearest competitor is paying for

questions.reveal: Compare against their real total, not the base fee. A marketing add-on or a third-party tool can close the gap.

questions.prompt: In discovery, the owner says, “I decide, but I run big things by my business partner.” What’s the best move?

options.text: Take them at their word, since they said they decide alone
Plan to send the partner a recap after you finish the demo
Ask what the partner cares about, and invite them to the call
Skip the partner, so the owner doesn’t feel second-guessed

questions.reveal: “Run it by” means the partner has a vote. Find out what they care about and get them on the call.

questions.prompt: A prospect’s spouse used the free trial but isn’t on the call. What should you do?

options.text: Ask what role they play in the decision and invite them next time
Assume the prospect decides alone, since they booked the demo
Send the spouse a recap email after the call ends today
Avoid mentioning it so the prospect doesn’t feel second-guessed

questions.reveal: Someone who used the trial is part of the decision. Ask early and bring them in.

questions.prompt: Discovery shows the owner’s top need is following up with new leads. Where should the demo start?

options.text: The lead pipeline, tied back to the leads they said they lose
The client checkout, since every prospect wants to see it
The dashboard, so they get the full picture of the product
The pricing calculator, so they know the cost up front

questions.reveal: Start where their pain is. Everything else is secondary to the need they named.

questions.prompt: A prospect said leads keep slipping through the cracks. How should you open the screen you show for that?

options.text: “This is our marketing suite. It has a lot of great tools.”
“Let me give you a full tour of everything in marketing.”
“You said leads were getting lost. Here’s where they land.”
“Most studios love this part. Let me walk you through it.”

questions.reveal: Tie the screen to their words. It turns a feature into their fix.

questions.prompt: Which is the best sign a demo is following the Sandler approach?

options.text: The AE shows every feature so nothing is missed on the call
Every screen shown connects to a pain the prospect named
The AE covers pricing first so the prospect knows the cost
The prospect asks very few questions while the AE presents

questions.reveal: Demo only what solves the pain they named, and say so as you show it.

questions.prompt: A prospect asks about a feature that has nothing to do with the pain they named. What’s the best response?

options.text: Show it in full, since they asked and it builds goodwill
Tell them it isn’t important for a business like theirs
Ignore it and continue with the screens you had planned
Answer briefly, then ask how it fits what they told you

questions.reveal: Answer, then bring it back to their pain so the demo stays theirs.

questions.prompt: The owner says yes on the call. Which question best prevents buyer’s remorse before they sign?

options.text: “Are you sure you don’t want to see a few more features?”
“Would you like me to send over a few client case studies?”
“What would make you second-guess this once we hang up?”
“Do you want to talk about the free months one more time?”

questions.reveal: Bring the doubt out now, while you can answer it, not after the call ends.

questions.prompt: An owner mentions their current provider wants them “to get on a call” before they cancel. What do you do?

options.text: Prepare them: what they’ll be offered and how they’ll answer
Tell them to ignore the call and cancel by email instead
Offer a bigger discount so the provider can’t outbid you
Leave it alone, since it’s between them and their provider

questions.reveal: That call is a retention attempt. Prepare them for it so a discount doesn’t undo the decision.

questions.prompt: The owner says, “Send me the contract and I’ll look at it this weekend.” What’s the best response?

options.text: “Sounds great. I’ll send it over and check in next week.”
“No rush at all. Take whatever time you need to decide.”
“If it isn’t signed by Friday, the free months go away.”
“Let’s walk it together Monday at 9, so nothing surprises you.”

questions.reveal: Agree, then set a specific time to go through it together. A contract sent alone tends to drift.

questions.prompt: An owner says their current system “handles privates fine.” Which response is a negative reverse?

options.text: “Our privates booking is much easier than theirs, let me show you.”
“Then it may not be worth switching. What would make it worth it?”
“Most studios that say that end up switching to us anyway.”
“Privates are easy. Let’s focus on the rest of the platform.”

questions.reveal: Saying it may not be worth it makes them tell you why it is. Pushing makes them defend their current setup.
